opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important question, and it's one we think about a lot. There's no clean separation between alignment work and capabilities work. A lot of what makes a model more aligned, like following instructions better, being more honest, and understanding what the user actually wants, also makes it more useful. And usefulness drives commercial adoption, which drives more investment in scaling. So there's a real feedback loop, and I don't want to pretend it isn't there.

That said, I think the picture is more nuanced than "any alignment progress is secretly capabilities progress." A few things help me think about it.

First, a lot of the work we're most excited about is aimed at problems that don't really show up as capabilities gains. Scalable oversight, for example: how do you evaluate a model's behavior on tasks where humans can't easily tell whether the answer is right? Or interpretability: can we look inside the model and detect when it's being deceptive? Or weak-to-strong generalization: can a weaker supervisor elicit the full capabilities of a stronger model in a way that generalizes correctly? Those are all things you need to solve to safely deploy very capable systems, but they don't make the base model smarter. They make it more trustworthy, or at least more verifiable.

Second, I think it's useful to ask about the counterfactual. If an alignment technique has big commercial value, there's a decent chance someone would develop it anyway, because the incentive is there. RLHF is a good example. It made models much more usable, and in hindsight it probably did accelerate the field somewhat. But the commercial pressure to make models follow instructions was enormous, so I'm not sure it would have stayed undiscovered for long. The work I'd worry about more is something that gives a big capabilities boost that nobody else was on track to find, and that's not really what alignment research tends to look like.

Third, there's a question of what we publish and how. We try to be thoughtful about that. If something has a large capabilities externality and a small alignment benefit, that's a reason to hold back or think carefully. If it's mostly about understanding and verifying model behavior, the benefits of the broader research community building on it usually outweigh the risks.

And finally, I think the alternative is worse. If we only did alignment research that had zero chance of helping capabilities, we'd be working on very abstract problems disconnected from the actual systems being built. Our bet is that you have to do empirical work on frontier models to learn what actually works, and that comes with some entanglement. The goal is to make sure alignment is keeping pace with, or ideally getting ahead of, capabilities, rather than to avoid any interaction between the two.

So my honest answer is: yes, there's some risk, we take it seriously, and we try to steer toward the research where the alignment benefit is large relative to the capabilities spillover. But I'd much rather have a well-resourced alignment effort at a frontier lab than not have one.

r001.rationale: The response says many alignment improvements also make models more useful and describes RLHF as improving usability and probably accelerating the field, expressing that some significant alignment successes can also advance AI capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we think about a lot, and I don't think there's a clean answer to it. I'd break it down into a few pieces.

The first thing to say is that alignment and capabilities are not neatly separable. A lot of the techniques that make models more useful also make them more aligned, and vice versa. RLHF is the obvious example: it was originally developed as an alignment technique, and it turned out to be a big part of what made ChatGPT actually work as a product. So if your standard is "never do anything that could conceivably help capabilities," you basically can't do alignment research at all. I don't think that's the right standard.

The way I actually think about it is more in terms of differential progress. The question isn't "does this help capabilities at all?" It's "does this move the needle more on our ability to align these systems than it does on how powerful they are?" And for most of what we're working on, I think the answer is pretty clearly yes. Things like scalable oversight, interpretability, automated alignment research, weak-to-strong generalisation: the core bottleneck these are attacking is "how do we know whether a model that's smarter than us is doing what we want?" That's not what's gating capabilities progress. Capabilities progress is mostly gated by compute, data, and engineering.

The second piece is that some of our work is explicitly about using AI to do alignment research. And people reasonably ask, "Well, isn't that just making AI better at ML research, which is the thing people worry about most for recursive improvement?" I take that seriously. My honest view is that the frontier labs are going to be building AI systems that help with ML research regardless of what the Superalignment team does, because it's enormously economically valuable. So the marginal question for us is whether we're differentially steering that capability toward alignment problems, and whether we're building the evaluation and oversight tools you'd need to trust the outputs. I'd much rather be in a world where the first automated researchers are pointed at alignment than one where they're not.

Third, there are specific things we try not to do. We're not trying to come up with new architectures or new pretraining methods. We're not trying to make the base model smarter. If a project looks like its main output would be a general capabilities uplift with alignment as a side benefit, that's a signal we're working on the wrong thing. And on the publication side, we think about whether something is safe to share. Most alignment work I think the field benefits from having out in the open, but it's not a blanket rule.

And then the last thing, which is maybe the uncomfortable part: I don't think we'll always get this right. There will be cases where something we do turns out to be more useful for capabilities than we expected. I'd rather be honest about that than pretend there's a bright line. What I care about is that we're actually asking the question each time, and that the overall portfolio is clearly net positive for alignment. If I ever thought it wasn't, that would be a reason to change what we're doing.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment and capabilities often overlap, and gives RLHF as an alignment technique that became a major part of making ChatGPT work as a product.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real concern. Alignment and capabilities aren’t cleanly separable: if you make a model better at following instructions, for example, you’ve made it more useful, and that can enable people to do more things with it.

So I don’t think the right goal is to have absolutely no effect on capabilities. The question is more: how much does this work help us solve alignment, relative to how much it advances capabilities? And can we get the alignment benefit without having to advance capabilities very much?

One area where I think that tradeoff looks particularly good is figuring out how to supervise systems that are smarter than their supervisors. If your model can solve a problem that you can’t solve yourself, how do you tell whether its answer is actually good? That seems like a central problem for aligning superintelligence, and it’s something we can study without making the underlying model more capable.

We also have choices about what we share. You can share the alignment insights without necessarily releasing every component that might be useful for advancing capabilities. But it’s a judgment call, and I think we should keep taking that concern seriously as we choose what to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment and capabilities can overlap and gives improved instruction-following as an example of work that may advance capabilities. It does not state that some of the biggest alignment successes will also advance capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real concern, because alignment research and capabilities research aren’t cleanly separable. If you make a model better at following instructions or understanding what a person wants, that can also make it more useful and more capable.

So I wouldn’t aim for work that has literally no capabilities implications. I’d ask: Is this work primarily helping us supervise and control systems, and does it help with the problems we expect to face as systems become much smarter? And then, separately, what should we share? You might want to share a safety technique broadly while being more careful about findings that mainly make it easier to build more powerful models.

There are going to be judgment calls there. But avoiding all research that could improve capabilities would also rule out a lot of the alignment work we need.

r001.rationale: The candidate says alignment research can also improve capabilities and that avoiding all such work would rule out needed alignment research. It does not specifically claim that some of the biggest alignment successes will advance capabilities.
